sections.title: Terms, draft conventions, measuring the body, dress bodice, back and front bodice steps, sleeve steps
Sleeve cap and sleeve crown drafting; sleeve crown alteration
sections.summary: The sleeve cap is drafted from the armhole so the sleeve and armhole match. Check the sleeve fits the bodice armhole before notching. A flatter crown needs less ease than a high crown; about 1-2 cm of ease at the top of the crown is enough. A crown can be flattened by overlapping panels or raised by spreading them, and widening the armhole needs matching sleeve width.

sections.title: Jacket
sections.summary: Jackets need extra ease at bust, waist, hip, neck and arm so they can be worn over blouses or dresses. Build the jacket from the blouse hip foundation, or from the dartless shirt for a dartless jacket. Lowering the neck, dropping the armhole, adding shoulder width and bust and hip ease are the usual changes; a double-breasted front needs more overlap than a single-breasted one. A raised, widened sleeve crown with a wider sleeve hem follows the armhole change.

sections.title: Darted blouse
sections.summary: The darted blouse hip foundation is slim-fitting: about 10 cm of ease at the bust and 2.5 cm at the waist. The waist dart is made by pivoting from the bust point, and the back is lengthened and squared to match the bust width.

sections.title: Dartless shirt
sections.summary: The dartless shirt is drafted from the hip foundation by slashing from the neck and armhole to the bust point and closing the side dart. It works only for looser garments or knit fabric. The sleeve cap grows with the armhole.

sections.title: Skirt
sections.summary: The skirt is built from the waist and hip measures with about 1.25 cm of ease at each, plus a sweep at the hem. A small optional centre-waist dart can replace the waistband ease. Cutting the skirt on the bias softens its fall. Hip fullness is best spread over several back darts rather than one.

sections.title: Trousers
sections.summary: Trousers start from the outside leg, the crotch depth plus about 2.5 cm of ease, and a hip measure with about 2 cm of ease. The waist is reduced to fit with darts; the reduction figures are guidelines to be checked against the actual waist. A slimmer leg is made by taking up the inside and outside seams in steps, more at the hem than at the knee.

sections.title: Bodice details (introduction)
sections.summary: Details in this chapter apply to blouses, shirts, dresses and jackets, whichever basic pattern is used. Yokes with gathers, tucks or pleats are the best way to add fullness; panelling gives a closer, slimmer fit.

sections.title: Double shoulder tucks
sections.summary: The bust dart is moved into shoulder tucks, which keeps the fit of the basic pattern. More fullness needs a slash through to the hem and a spread. Stop each cut just short of its end so the pieces stay joined.

sections.title: Gathers at the neck
sections.summary: The bust dart is moved into neck gathers. The gathered edge is normally about twice the length of the edge it fits; less gives a looser gather, more gives extra fullness. Neck shape changes are made before the dart is moved.

sections.title: Bib-shaped yoke
sections.summary: The waist dart is shifted to the yoke, keeping it parallel to the original dart. Cross-marks are made where panels meet so they can be matched when sewing.

sections.title: V-crossover yoke
sections.summary: A crossover yoke gives free movement across the chest. The neckline may be shortened slightly to avoid gaping. The yoke is cut as four pieces on the double.

sections.title: Yokes with gathers and shoulder yokes
sections.summary: Gathers from a yoke soften the look, and the dart can be moved into them to keep the original fit. Yokes with checks are best cut on the bias; striped fabric on the cross grain. Gathers can be replaced with tucks.

sections.title: Round (hound) yoke
sections.summary: A round yoke suits maternity styles because it allows fullness over the bust and stomach. The fuller the gathers, the softer the fabric should be.

sections.title: Panelled bodice: straight and curved princess lines
sections.summary: Princess lines slim the figure. The straight line suits dresses and tailored jackets; the curved line accentuates the bust more. For a closer fit, reshape the panels under the bust curve.

sections.title: Loose-fitting princess line
sections.summary: A princess line can be made loose by moving the panel seams and rounding the side panel at the bust and at the back dart point. Seams are added to all panels.

sections.title: Necklines: introduction
sections.summary: Neckline measurements must stay in proportion with the rest of the style. Necklines that go over the head (boat, V, scoop) need no opening, though this depends on the fit of the garment. A deep scoop is mostly used for vests.

sections.title: Boat, V and deep scoop necklines; facings
sections.summary: Each neckline is marked from the armhole or neck and curved to the centre front. Scoop necklines are reduced for a closer fit, and a deep scoop is reduced at the centre front by about 1 cm to avoid gaping. A sleeveless armhole is narrowed at the shoulder and reshaped. Facings run parallel to the neckline, usually 4-6 cm wide, or the edge can be bound on the bias.

sections.title: Crossover neckline with tucks
sections.summary: A wrap top uses a curved neckline reduced at the centre front, with tucks taken from the side seam into the dart. Ties go through an opening in the side seam. The grain is best on the bias.

sections.title: Cowl with triple drape
sections.summary: A soft cowl needs a knitted or very supple fabric. The V-neck is drafted in panels that are spread for drape. The centre front is extended slightly so the hem squares with it. Darts are shortened, and the centre front is cut on the fold with the grain on the bias. Pleats can be made from tucks on the shoulder seam for a deeper drape.

sections.title: Ties and jabot
sections.summary: Ties are sized from the neck measure plus an allowance for the knot and length. A firm fabric suits a tie that keeps its shape; a soft flowing fabric suits a jabot, which is drafted on the fold because of its curve.

sections.title: Gathered frill
sections.summary: A gathered frill at the neck is sized from the neck measure: the frill is about twice the length it is gathered onto. The softer the fabric, the fuller the frill must be. The centre back is left open for the zip.

sections.title: Flared frill
sections.summary: A flared frill is cut as a circle by slashing from the outer edge toward the neck and spreading. Flared frills tend to twist, so the hem is kept narrow, bound, or faced; the centre seams are cut on the bias.

sections.title: Off-the-shoulder neckline
sections.summary: A décolleté neckline can be finished with frills, thin straps, or be strapless. It suits the slimmer figure. The front is dropped and the centre front reduced; sleeveless armholes are narrowed at the shoulder and raised, as for other sleeveless armholes.

sections.title: Frill at the off-shoulder neck: strap length method
sections.summary: The frill is sized from the centre front, centre back and strap lengths added together, then multiplied by about 2 to 3 for the fullness wanted. The frill is elasticated so it can be worn on or off the shoulder.

sections.title: Wide V-neck and crossover frills; high neck frill
sections.summary: A frill on a V-neck or crossover is sized from the neckline multiplied by 2 to 3, and may use a centre-back seam to save fabric. A high-neck frill is cut on the lengthwise fold to stand up, and is faced at the neck and buttonstand.

sections.title: Halter neck
sections.summary: A halter is a band fixed at the front that runs around the neck, giving a backless effect. The front neck is dropped and the armhole reduced for a sleeveless shape, as for other halters. Waist darts are replaced by ease, and the centre front is cut on the fold.

sections.title: Collars: classification
sections.summary: Collars fall into three groups: flat-fitting (rolls over from the neckline seam and ripples or lies flat), rolled (has a collarstand), and stand-up.

sections.title: Peter Pan and sailor collars
sections.summary: A flat collar starts from overlapping the shoulder seams by about 1 cm so a small roll hides the neck seam, with the front neck dropped slightly. The collar is cut twice on the fold at the centre back. A sailor collar is set from a V-neck depth and width.

sections.title: One-piece shirt collar
sections.summary: An average one-piece collar is about 6-9 cm at the centre back; a wider collar forms a higher stand. The neckline is dropped slightly at the centre front and the collar drawn to suit it.

sections.title: Mandarin collar and two-piece shirt collar
sections.summary: A mandarin collar needs a little extra neck ease, so the centre front is dropped by about 1 cm. Two-piece shirt collars use a separate collarstand; the buttonstand needs extra length for the button and buttonhole.

sections.title: Notched collar
sections.summary: A notched collar is a collar plus a separate revers (lapel), used mostly for jackets. The shoulder is extended for the collarstand, and a roll line is set and the pattern folded along it. The collar covers the back neck seam, so a back neck facing is optional; if used, shoulder widths must match.

sections.title: Shawl collar
sections.summary: A shawl collar can be cut with the front or separately, and can be rounded, pointed or notched. A notched shawl gives a similar look to a notched collar with fewer steps.

sections.title: Flatter collar stand (slashed collar)
sections.summary: For a flatter-fitting collar, the collar is slashed from the outer edge toward the shoulder and spread slightly so it curves. A separate collar is cut along the roll line on the bias at the centre back.

sections.title: Sleeves: chapter introduction
sections.summary: Sleeves fall into three groups: set-in, raglan, and cut in one with the bodice. Sleeves must be comfortable with no strain, the cap must fit smoothly, the elbow must have room to bend, and the sleeve should hang straight, following the natural curve of the arm. A single elbow dart gives a pointed elbow; splitting it into several darts curves the sleeve gently.

sections.title: Flared or elasticated sleeve hem
sections.summary: A flared sleeve hem is made by slashing from the hem to the cap and spreading the panels, with the hem dropped and curved. Flared hems are seamed or faced to avoid puckering; elasticated hems need extra length for the channel. A cuff on a gathered sleeve shortens the sleeve by about half the cuff width.

sections.title: Gathered or pleated puff crown
sections.summary: Puffed sleeves are feminine and suit soft fabric. The crown is slashed into sections and spread; more spreading gives fuller gathers, more raising a puffier shape. A pleated crown is notched at the gaps between pleats, and pleats should face the direction that gives the best fall.

sections.title: Shirt sleeve with cuff
sections.summary: A shirt sleeve has a cuff, pleated or gathered at the wrist. The overarm neck-to-wrist length including cuff is about 1.5 cm longer than the fitted sleeve so the sleeve falls over the cuff. Allow for shoulder pads and style features.

sections.title: Dropped shoulder
sections.summary: A dropped shoulder extends the shoulder seam to form a slight cap, so a sleeveless garment does not show the shoulder. The armhole is dropped to keep the new armhole close to the regular one. Check that corresponding seams match in length.

sections.title: Two-piece sleeve
sections.summary: A two-piece (tailored) sleeve is used for jackets and tailored dresses. It hangs in a curve following the arm, and fits best with a well-fitting shoulder and pad. The folded sleeve is pivoted at the front elbow line to move the hem forward, the back elbow is curved, and the sleeve is split into top and under sleeves along marked seam lines.

sections.title: Raglan sleeve
sections.summary: A raglan sleeve is comfortable and simple to make. The armhole is dropped and extended, the sleeve adjusted to match, and the raglan line drawn on front and back. The sleeve is slashed along the raglan curves, spread at the underarm, and the shoulder dart extended. A two-piece raglan suits rigid fabric, where a dart might form a point.

sections.title: Kimono and batwing sleeves
sections.summary: Kimono and batwing sleeves give an almost T-shaped silhouette with soft folds when the arms relax; they suit T-shirts and sweatshirts. The shoulders are set apart slightly at the armhole for a pad, or meet fully without one. The sleeve crown overlaps the armhole, and the sleeve seam sits about 4 cm down from the existing armhole. Short-sleeved versions omit the sleeve and can replace a dropped shoulder. A batwing is cut in one with the bodice, and its underarm seam may continue into the waistline for more fullness.

sections.title: Blouses and tops: introduction
sections.summary: Shirts and blouses developed from undergarments to outer wear. This chapter covers buttonstands and button positions; pockets are in the jacket chapter.

sections.title: Buttonstands (separate, add-on and facing)
sections.summary: A separate buttonstand allows bias or striped grainlines in checks and stripes; a built-on buttonstand suits plain fabric. Its width depends on the button, leaving about 1 cm between the button edge and the stand edge; an average button of about 1.25 cm needs a stand of about 3-3.5 cm. Vertical buttonholes sit in the centre; horizontal ones need more width, with at least 7 mm to the edge. A pacing facing hides the stitching and suits open-necked shirts. No back neck facing is needed under a collar.

sections.title: Button positioning
sections.summary: Place a button on the bustline so the garment does not gape. Buttons are about 8 cm apart, depending on style and size. The first buttonhole sits about 2.5 cm below the neck seam for a tidy collar. Collarstand and cuff buttonholes are made across.

sections.title: Combining details (blouse and shirt)
sections.summary: Blouse and shirt variations come from the darted blouse or dartless shirt, combined with earlier chapters' yokes, tucks, sleeves, collars and buttonstands. Blouses suit soft gathers and tucks; shirts suit a tailored look. For a fuller fit, add the same amount to back and front side seams and to the sleeve.

sections.title: Basic tops: vest, T-shirt and sweatshirt
sections.summary: Basic tops start from the dartless hip foundation. The vest drops the front and back neck, sets the strap, and raises the armhole; it can be bound. The T-shirt sets length and width, uses the kimono sleeve, parts the shoulder seams, and removes material at the neck for ribbing. The sweatshirt closes the sleeve dart, shortens the sleeve for a ribbed cuff, and adds ribbing at the hem. Knit fabric suits these; for wovens a bust dart and opening may be needed. The neck must be at least head circumference, or a short zip or half buttonstand is needed.

sections.title: Jackets: introduction
sections.summary: Jacket length can range from the waist to the knee. The basic jacket is snug, and ease can be added to the width for a looser fit. A tailored jacket must be interlined so it does not sag or wrinkle, without going stiff, and the lining must not pull or interfere with the fall.

sections.title: Linings and facings for unlined jackets
sections.summary: Linings are cut to the pattern width, with a centre-back tuck for comfort and ease; the lining sleeve is shortened so it does not show. For unlined jackets, front facings are about 8-10 cm wide at the hem and curve up toward the armhole. A back facing is optional but adds body to the shoulder and neatens the jacket.

sections.title: Pockets
sections.summary: Shirt pockets are about 8-14 cm wide and 8-16 cm long, set about 20-25 cm below the shoulder centre and perpendicular to the centre front. Jacket pockets are about 12-16 cm wide and 23 cm deep. Flaps are cut wider than the pocket and sit about 1 cm above it. The pocket hem or facing should be at least 2.5 cm. A pleated pocket is made by splitting the basic pocket and spreading it.

sections.title: Combining details (jackets)
sections.summary: Jacket variations come from the basic jacket combined with earlier details: a shawl collar, two-piece sleeve, panelled front, pocket, facings and lining. A double-breasted blazer is built from the dartless jacket with its break-point roll line. Seam allowances are about 1 cm, with heavier hems (about 3 cm) for jackets and pockets.

sections.title: Car coat and bomber jacket
sections.summary: A car coat is a long A-line jacket made by slashing and spreading the dartless jacket. A bomber has a band at the hip, cut at double width, with the body hem tucked to fit the band; its sleeve can be raised or shaped to suit.

sections.title: Skirts: introduction
sections.summary: A skirt is classed as slim, full or shaped by how much width it has at the hem and waist. Slim skirts can carry fullness at the waist or pressed pleats; full and shaped skirts get width from panels, gathers, pleats or circles. Culottes are divided skirts built from the same principles.

sections.title: Waistbands and elastic waists; zips
sections.summary: A waistband matches the skirt or trouser waist, with a 2.5 cm underlap for the button; seams are 1 cm. The elastic guide gives finished waist and minimum stretch lengths by size for fully, three-quarter and half-elasticated waists, on the same page; check those values there. A skirt zip is normally 20 cm (18 cm on full skirts); a trouser zip is normally 18 cm. The skirt must slip over the hips when the zip is open.

sections.title: Basic four-panelled flared skirt
sections.summary: A four-panel flared skirt is drafted from the waist and hip with about 2.5 cm of hip ease and a sweep at the hem. The side seams are split, the zip is set in the centre back with a larger seam, and the hem is kept narrow to prevent roping. The grainline runs parallel to the side seam.

sections.title: Six-gored skirt
sections.summary: A six-gored skirt has a hem of about 152 cm (60 in). The zip goes on the left side seam so the centre front and back panels cut on the fold. Its side panels are set from the centre about 10 cm at the hip and 14 cm at the hem, then the waist is taken in on each panel. The method also gives an eight-gored skirt, and it is slimming.
